action_schema.notes: avoid action_type always has empty adjustment and adjustment_type. sowing and harvesting use only 'delay' as adjustment. Not Feasible entries carry exactly one action with action_type 'avoid'. Ideal entries carry an empty actions array.

soil_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: Clay > Loamy > Sandy | Maize: Loamy > Sandy > Clay | Cotton: Loamy > Sandy > Clay

Clay.reasoning: Clay retains water through natural puddling, maintaining flooded paddy conditions while its high cation exchange capacity supports season-long fertility.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam provides adequate water retention and nutrient cycling for rice with consistent irrigation and field bunding to maintain paddy water levels.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil cannot retain standing water, making flooded paddy conditions impractical and uneconomical even with intensive irrigation.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam's balance of drainage, aeration and moisture retention provides optimal conditions for vigorous maize development.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil drains too rapidly, causing nutrient leaching and moisture stress that reduce maize yield without compensating irrigation and fertiliser inputs.

Clay.reasoning: Clay's poor aeration causes oxygen deficiency in maize roots within 24–48 hours, leading to root rot and growth collapse.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam supports cotton's deep taproot with good drainage and aeration, enabling strong boll development and high fibre quality.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil's low nutrient retention undermines cotton's high fertility demands during boll development without active replenishment.

Clay.reasoning: Clay's chronic saturation promotes Pythium root rot in cotton and causes boll shedding under prolonged wet conditions.

season_adjustment_rules._note: Sowing suitability score per season (0-1). High = good sowing window.

Rainy.reasoning: Monsoon rainfall directly maintains flooded paddy conditions, reducing irrigation demand while warm temperatures and high humidity support all rice growth stages.

Winter.reasoning: Winter cold falls below rice's germination threshold and cannot supply the water availability paddy cultivation requires.

Summer.reasoning: Summer rice achieves high yields with irrigation; warm temperatures drive rapid grain fill and heat-tolerant varieties manage heat stress at flowering.

Fall.reasoning: Declining autumn temperatures and rainfall prevent rice from completing its growing cycle in this season.

Rainy.reasoning: Consistent rainy-season rainfall and warmth support all maize growth stages, delivering strong yields when planting avoids peak-flooding low-lying fields.

Winter.reasoning: Winter cold falls below maize's germination threshold and frost risk prevents seedling establishment in most growing regions.

Summer.reasoning: Summer's high temperatures and long days maximise C4 photosynthesis in maize, delivering peak yield potential with appropriate irrigation.

Fall.reasoning: Cooling autumn temperatures and irregular rainfall cause poor germination and insufficient heat accumulation to complete the maize crop cycle.

Rainy.reasoning: The rainy Kharif season is cotton's natural growing window; warmth and moisture support vigorous establishment and boll development over its long crop duration.

Winter.reasoning: Cotton's frost sensitivity and long growing cycle make winter cultivation infeasible in all but tropical frost-free regions.

Summer.reasoning: Summer heat and high solar radiation drive boll maturation and peak fibre quality, making it cotton's most productive season with supplemental irrigation.

Fall.reasoning: Cotton's long season cannot complete before autumn cold arrives; frost risk during boll maturation devastates yield and fibre quality.

temperature_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: warm but suffers in extreme heat | Maize: balanced, sensitive at flowering | Cotton: loves heat

15-20.reasoning: Sub-optimal temperatures inhibit rice germination, delay tillering and cause pollen sterility at flowering; thermal accumulation is insufficient for grain fill.

20-30.reasoning: The 20–30°C range is optimal for rice, supporting rapid tillering, efficient photosynthesis and high grain fill rates.

30-40.reasoning: Heat above 30°C during flowering causes pollen sterility and reduces grain set; increased irrigation and adjusted sowing dates limit yield loss.

15-20.reasoning: Cool temperatures slow germination and risk chilling injury at seedling stage; sowing should be delayed until soils warm sufficiently.

20-30.reasoning: Optimal range for maize, supporting vigorous vegetative growth, efficient nutrient uptake and successful pollination.

30-40.reasoning: Heat above 30°C reduces pollen viability at tasselling and silking, causing 5–8% yield loss per degree; irrigation and adjusted planting dates are critical.

15-20.reasoning: Below 18°C soil temperature cotton cannot germinate; this range prevents crop establishment and fibre development entirely.

20-30.reasoning: Below cotton's 30–35°C optimum, yields are 15–20% lower and boll development is slower; balanced fertilisation and sowing timing partially compensate.

30-40.reasoning: Cotton's optimal thermal range accelerates boll maturation and maximises fibre quality; maintain irrigation and monitor for spider mites in hot, dry conditions.

humidity_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: high humidity lover >70% | Maize: balanced, prefers medium | Cotton: dry climate, prefers low-medium

<40.reasoning: Very dry air accelerates transpiration from paddies, causing leaf water deficit and poor grain fill; incompatible with productive paddy cultivation.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity raises rice's irrigation requirements; adequate yields are possible with closer water management to offset elevated transpiration.

>70.reasoning: High humidity minimises transpiration stress and supports the moist microclimate required for optimal rice growth and grain development.

<40.reasoning: Low humidity elevates evapotranspiration and moisture stress risk at silking and grain fill; proactive irrigation prevents yield-reducing deficits.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity balances moisture availability and disease risk, providing optimal growing conditions for maize across its life cycle.

>70.reasoning: High humidity promotes northern leaf blight and grey leaf spot; avoid overhead irrigation that wets foliage and favour disease-resistant varieties.

<40.reasoning: Very low humidity raises cotton's water demand sharply, causing boll shedding without consistent root-zone moisture; drip irrigation and mulching are essential.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity supports healthy boll development with low fungal disease pressure; monitor for early disease signs as humidity approaches 70%.

>70.reasoning: Persistent high humidity causes boll rot, Alternaria blight and bacterial blight that devastate cotton fibre yield and quality.

soil_moisture_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: high/flooded | Maize: moderate well-drained | Cotton: moderate avoids excess

<30.reasoning: Below 30% volumetric moisture, flooded paddy conditions cannot be established and rice fails to develop the anaerobic root environment it requires.

30-60.reasoning: Moderate moisture falls below rice's saturation requirement; frequent irrigation must actively establish and maintain standing water for acceptable yields.

>60.reasoning: Near-saturated soil replicates natural paddy conditions, supporting the anaerobic root microenvironment and weed suppression rice requires.

<30.reasoning: Below 30% volumetric moisture, permanent wilting begins in maize leaf tissue; irrigation at critical stages prevents lasting yield loss.

30-60.reasoning: Moderately moist, well-drained soil provides optimal aeration and water availability for maize root development and nutrient uptake.

>60.reasoning: Waterlogging deprives maize roots of oxygen within 48 hours, causing root rot, nitrogen loss and rapid yield collapse even in short flooding events.

<30.reasoning: Moisture below 30% during boll development causes premature shedding; targeted irrigation at critical stages maintains productivity.

30-60.reasoning: Moderate soil moisture sustains boll filling and supports cotton's deep taproot without the waterlogging risk that triggers root disease.

>60.reasoning: Saturated soil causes Pythium and Phytophthora root rot in cotton; boll drop and fibre staining make production unviable under prolonged wet conditions.

ph_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: Acidic~Neutral > Alkaline | Maize: Neutral >> others | Cotton: Neutral >= Alkaline > Acidic

Acidic.reasoning: Rice is well adapted to acidic soils and benefits from increased iron and manganese availability in flooded conditions; high yields are achievable at pH above 4.5.

Neutral.reasoning: Neutral pH maximises nutrient availability and microbial activity, supporting efficient nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium uptake in rice.

Alkaline.reasoning: Alkaline conditions reduce iron and zinc availability in rice, causing deficiency symptoms that reduce grain yield without targeted micronutrient correction.

Acidic.reasoning: Acidic soils cause aluminium and manganese toxicity in maize and reduce phosphorus availability; liming and phosphorus supplementation are required.

Neutral.reasoning: Neutral pH (6.0–7.0) optimises all nutrient availability and microbial nitrogen fixation, providing ideal conditions for maize.

Alkaline.reasoning: Alkaline soils cause iron, zinc and manganese deficiency in maize, producing chlorosis and stunted growth without chelated micronutrient correction.

Acidic.reasoning: Low pH causes aluminium toxicity and phosphorus deficiency in cotton, limiting boll set; lime and phosphorus supplementation are required.

Neutral.reasoning: Neutral pH delivers optimal availability of all nutrients needed for cotton's growth, boll filling and fibre development.

Alkaline.reasoning: Cotton tolerates mild alkalinity well and performs at normal yield levels up to pH 8.0; targeted micronutrient supplementation easily manages any deficiencies above this level.

sunlight_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: sensitive to extreme heat | Maize: thrives in strong sunlight | Cotton: prefers long sunny periods

<4.reasoning: Fewer than 4 hours reduces photosynthesis in rice, causing poor tillering and reduced grain fill; nitrogen support partially offsets the energy shortfall.

4-8.reasoning: Four to eight hours meets rice's photosynthetic requirements at all growth stages, supporting tillering, grain development and yield.

>8.reasoning: High sunlight boosts dry matter accumulation in rice with adequate water supply; increased irrigation offsets the higher evapotranspiration demand.

<4.reasoning: Fewer than 4 hours is insufficient for maize's C4 photosynthesis rate; reduced crop density and balanced fertilisation help maximise limited-light yield.

4-8.reasoning: Good light drives the high photosynthetic rate maize requires for rapid vegetative growth and full cob development.

>8.reasoning: Full sun maximises maize biomass production and kernel filling, especially during grain fill, delivering peak yield potential.

<4.reasoning: Cotton requires high light intensity for boll development; fewer than 4 hours causes excessive boll shedding and poor fibre quality regardless of other inputs.

4-8.reasoning: Four to eight hours provides adequate light for cotton boll development and fibre maturation; appropriate spacing and variety selection deliver competitive yields.

>8.reasoning: High sunlight maximises cotton photosynthesis and accelerates boll maturation for peak fibre yield and quality; maintain irrigation to match elevated evapotranspiration.

irrigation_frequency_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: frequent/continuous | Maize: moderate controlled | Cotton: low-frequency drought-tolerant

<2.reasoning: Fewer than 2 irrigations per week cannot maintain the standing water rice paddies require for weed suppression and productive paddy culture.

3-4.reasoning: Three to four irrigations per week supports productive rice using AWD techniques, maintaining adequate moisture while reducing water use by up to 30% versus continuous flooding.

>5.reasoning: Frequent irrigation maintains the flooded or near-saturated conditions that rice requires, suppresses weeds and supports consistent grain filling.

<2.reasoning: Infrequent irrigation risks moisture stress at tasselling and silking; applying larger volumes per event extends the effective moisture window between irrigations.

3-4.reasoning: Moderate irrigation frequency provides consistent moisture for maize without waterlogging risk, matching weekly evapotranspiration demand.

>5.reasoning: Over-frequent irrigation promotes shallow roots, nutrient leaching and root rot; reducing volume and moving to soil-moisture-based scheduling improves root depth and soil health.

<2.reasoning: Cotton needs minimum root-zone moisture for boll formation; fewer than 2 irrigations per week risks boll shedding and requires efficient drip delivery to extend moisture availability.

3-4.reasoning: Three to four irrigations per week supports consistent boll development in cotton with good drainage to prevent root-zone saturation.

>5.reasoning: Excessively high frequency saturates cotton's root zone, creating conditions for Pythium root rot and widespread boll shedding that make cultivation unviable.

water_source_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: continuous/high | Maize: controlled moderate | Cotton: precise low-frequency

River.reasoning: Abundant, continuous river supply maintains flooded paddy conditions throughout the season with naturally mineralised water.

Groundwater.reasoning: Reliable and clean groundwater enables precise AWD-based scheduling for rice, offering dependable supply with controlled delivery.

Recycled.reasoning: Recycled water risks pathogen and heavy metal transfer to edible rice grain; food safety concerns make it unacceptable for paddy cultivation.

River.reasoning: River water provides reliable, mineralised supply for maize; controlled furrow or drip delivery prevents over-irrigation.

Groundwater.reasoning: Groundwater enables precise, on-demand irrigation matching maize's moderate water requirements without timing or flood constraints.

Recycled.reasoning: Recycled water is usable for maize with EC and pathogen monitoring; rotation with fresh water prevents progressive salt accumulation in soil.

River.reasoning: River water is adequate for cotton but harder to volume-control with gravity systems, requiring furrow management criteria to avoid over-irrigation.

Groundwater.reasoning: Groundwater's precision delivery matches cotton's low-frequency needs and minimises wet-foliage disease risk.

Recycled.reasoning: Recycled water is more acceptable for non-food cotton fibre but salt content risks germination and boll set; limited, monitored application is essential.

<50.reasoning: Below 50mm cannot support maize germination or root development without heavy supplemental irrigation.

50-100.reasoning: Below minimum for rainfed maize; supplemental irrigation is critical at germination and tasselling to prevent moisture stress and yield failure.

100-200.reasoning: Optimal rainfall supports germination, vegetative growth and grain fill without waterlogging risk.

200-300.reasoning: Upper optimal range; maize performs well with reduced supplemental irrigation and standard drainage management.

>300.reasoning: Excessive rainfall creates waterlogging and root rot risk; immediate drainage management is required to prevent yield loss.

<50.reasoning: Below 50mm is wholly insufficient for paddy without a reliable irrigation source capable of maintaining 5–10cm standing water.

50-100.reasoning: Well below paddy requirements; heavy supplemental irrigation is essential during transplanting and tillering to maintain standing water depth.

100-200.reasoning: Moderate rainfall reduces but does not eliminate irrigation demand; supplemental water is still needed to maintain adequate paddy depth throughout the season.

200-300.reasoning: Optimal rainfall sustains flooded paddy with minimal supplemental irrigation, supporting high tiller production and grain fill.

>300.reasoning: High rainfall benefits paddy rice; manage drainage to prevent over-flooding above 15cm and avoid nitrogen top-dressing during heavy rain to prevent leaching.

<50.reasoning: Below 50mm, boll shedding risk is high without reliable irrigation at every critical growth stage from sowing through boll fill.

50-100.reasoning: Below-optimal rainfall requires supplemental irrigation at squaring and boll fill to prevent premature shedding and yield loss.

100-200.reasoning: Optimal rainfall supports strong vegetative growth and full boll development with minimal supplemental irrigation.

200-300.reasoning: Above-optimal rainfall increases boll rot and fungal disease risk; all supplemental irrigation should cease and field drainage should be improved.

>300.reasoning: Excessive rainfall causes boll rot, fibre staining and root disease that significantly compromise yield and quality.
